title: Spielberg Revisits His Films as Poltergeist and Hook Return
excerpt: Steven Spielberg's legacy returns to focus through Poltergeist streaming, his criticism of Temple of Doom, and a live orchestral screening of Hook.
content:
Steven Spielberg's filmmaking career is attracting renewed attention through several developments involving his classic movies, creative disagreements, and long-standing musical collaborations. The 1982 horror film Poltergeist is available on free streaming, while his criticism of Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom and an upcoming orchestral presentation of Hook highlight different sides of his work.

These developments also revisit Spielberg's relationship with fellow filmmaker Tobe Hooper and composer John Williams, whose collaborations helped shape some of Hollywood's most recognizable productions.

Poltergeist, originally released in 1982, became available for free streaming on Pluto TV on November 1, according to Polygon. The supernatural horror story follows a suburban family whose home becomes the center of increasingly disturbing paranormal events.

The family's youngest child, five-year-old Carol Anne, played by Heather O'Rourke, begins communicating with mysterious beings through the television. The situation escalates when supernatural forces take her into another dimension, prompting her family to seek assistance from paranormal investigators.

Although Tobe Hooper received the official directing credit, Spielberg's extensive involvement in the production has fueled decades of discussion about who actually controlled the filmmaking process.

Spielberg originally developed an extraterrestrial horror concept called Night Skies after completing Close Encounters of the Third Kind. He eventually transformed much of that creative direction into E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial, while Hooper became involved in the development of Poltergeist.

However, the accounts of their respective contributions differ. Hooper maintained that Poltergeist originated from an independent idea he had developed, while other accounts connected the project to Spielberg's abandoned extraterrestrial concept.

John Leonetti, who worked as a camera assistant, described Spielberg as the person effectively directing the production. Actors JoBeth Williams and Craig T. Nelson, who portrayed the parents, maintained that Hooper directed the film, although they acknowledged Spielberg's substantial involvement as producer.

Zelda Rubinstein, who played paranormal medium Tangina Barrons, characterized the production as a joint effort, with Spielberg exercising greater control.

In a 1982 interview with The Los Angeles Times, Spielberg described how their working relationship developed during production.

"Tobe isn't what you'd call a take-charge sort of guy. He's just not a strong presence on a movie set. If a question was asked and an answer wasn't immediately forthcoming, I'd jump up and say what we could do.

Tobe would nod agreement, and that became the process of the collaboration." Spielberg said.

The controversy also involved the film's marketing. Poltergeist and E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial arrived in 1982, leading to considerable attention around Spielberg's filmmaking activities. MGM and United Artists emphasized his involvement in promotional campaigns, sometimes overshadowing Hooper's official directing position.

The Directors Guild investigated the situation and concluded that the studio had diminished Hooper's directing credit. The studio subsequently had to pay him $15,000.

Spielberg's own assessment of his earlier productions also resurfaced in a separate report by Far Out Magazine. He expressed dissatisfaction with Indiana Jones and the Temple of Doom, the 1984 sequel to Raiders of the Lost Ark.

Although the film achieved substantial commercial success, Spielberg considered its darker atmosphere inconsistent with his personal filmmaking preferences.

"I wasn't happy with Temple of Doom at all. It was too dark, too subterranean, and much too horrific. I thought it out-poltered Poltergeist.

There's not an ounce of my own personal feeling in Temple of Doom. The danger in making a sequel is that you can never satisfy everyone." Spielberg said.

He also described the difficulty of balancing audience expectations with the desire to create something different from the original film.

"You lose both ways." Spielberg said.

The director's comments came against the background of a career that includes major commercial and critical successes. His films include Jaws, Close Encounters of the Third Kind, Raiders of the Lost Ark, E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial, Jurassic Park, Schindler's List, and Saving Private Ryan.

Meanwhile, Spielberg declined to identify four favorite films when questioned by Letterboxd at the MoMA Film Benefit, according to AOL UK. The filmmaker explained that choosing a limited number could create unnecessary disappointment among colleagues whose movies he also appreciated.

"I don't have four favourite films." Spielberg said.

He expanded on his reluctance to rank filmmakers and their work.

"I can never answer that question. I have 20 friends who have made movies this year. I'm not going to name four of them, and then have to deal with the other 16 I didn't mention." Spielberg said.

Separately, Spielberg's partnership with composer John Williams will receive renewed attention through a live presentation of Hook with the San Francisco Symphony. The performances are scheduled for November 27 at 7:30 p.m. and November 28 at 2 p.m. at Davies Symphony Hall in San Francisco.

The 1991 fantasy film stars Robin Williams as an adult Peter Pan who has forgotten Neverland, with Dustin Hoffman portraying Captain James Hook. Maggie Smith, Julia Roberts, and Bob Hoskins also appear in the production.

Conductor Sarah Hicks, who will lead the orchestra, said Williams' musical contribution was central to her appreciation of the movie.

"I think it's one of John's greatest scores." Hicks said.

Williams created an elaborate musical structure featuring more than a dozen interconnected themes and recurring motifs. The orchestration uses horns to communicate adventure, strings to evoke childhood memories, and flutes associated with Peter Pan's character.

The original creative plans also included musical elements. Spielberg and Williams initially considered making Hook a musical, working with lyricist Leslie Bricusse, although the concept eventually changed.

Three songs remained in the finished production: We Don't Wanna Grow Up, Pick 'em Up, and When You're Alone, which received an Academy Award nomination.

Hicks explained how the original songs became part of the film's orchestral identity.

"It's such an interesting score because they transferred some of those songs into (orchestral) form. There's something about it that captures you even more because there's these incredible melodies to latch onto." Hicks said.

She also highlighted the film's adult themes, particularly its treatment of lost childhood memories, regret, and the responsibilities associated with growing up.

"It's a kids film, but it's also a very adult film about these themes of regret and loss of innocence and this whole trope of the yuppie cult. It's a reminder of a time when you could have a view of the world in which you can fly. I think we all wish for that in some ways." Hicks said.

The San Francisco Symphony's Hook performances will present the film alongside Williams' orchestral score on November 27 and 28 at Davies Symphony Hall.
